---
title: "Recurring techniques"
---

The same building blocks come back in many charts. This chapter explains
each of them once, and the chart pages link here. You can read it straight
through, or look things up when a chart page sends you here.

## Plotting functions you will meet

| Call | Draws |
|---|---|
| `ax.plot(x, y)` | A line (or, with `marker=` and `linestyle="none"`, markers only) |
| `ax.bar(x, heights)` | Vertical bars |
| `ax.scatter(x, y)` | Dots |
| `ax.fill_between(x, lower, upper)` | A shaded area between two lines |
| `ax.axhline(y)` / `ax.axvline(x)` | A horizontal / vertical line across the whole plot |
| `ax.hlines(y, x0, x1)` / `ax.vlines(x, y0, y1)` | Short horizontal / vertical line pieces |
| `ax.text(x, y, "text")` | Text |
| `ax.annotate("text", xy=..., xytext=...)` | Text with a line or arrow pointing at something |
| `ax.legend(...)` | The legend |

Most functions take the same styling arguments:

- `color=` takes a hex code such as `"#0067A5"` or a name such as `"black"`.
- `linewidth=` is in points.
- `label=` is the name shown in the legend.
- `zorder=` sets what is drawn on top of what (higher is on top).

## Categories as positions {#sec-categories}

When the x-axis shows text, such as quarters (`2024Q1`) or country names,
Excel spaces the categories evenly. The scripts do the same by plotting
against the positions 0, 1, 2, ... and then putting the text under those
positions:

```python
x = np.arange(len(data))                         # 0, 1, 2, ..., one per row
ax.plot(x, data["USA"])
ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)  # a label under each position
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)               # half a step of room at each end
```

`np.arange(n)` is numpy's version of 0, 1, ..., n-1. `rotation=90` turns the
labels vertical, as in many REO charts.

For bar charts, the first bar is often at 1 instead of 0 (`np.arange(1,
len(data) + 1)`). That makes the positions of separators between bars easy
to write down: 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and so on.

**Years** are numbers, so charts with annual data plot against the years
themselves (`ax.plot(data["category"], ...)`). The limits are then years too,
e.g. `ax.set_xlim(2018.5, 2026.5)`.

Used in: [1.1](charts/fig-1-1.qmd), [2.1](charts/fig-2-1.qmd),
[2.4](charts/fig-2-4.qmd), [3.3](charts/fig-3-3.qmd),
[5.2](charts/fig-5-2.qmd) and all bar charts.

## Dates on the x-axis {#sec-dates}

Daily and monthly data come in as real dates. matplotlib places them on a
time axis, so gaps and uneven spacing are handled correctly:

```python
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import pandas as pd

START, END = pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2026-09-30")
data = data[(data["category"] >= START) & (data["category"] <= END)]   # keep the shown period

ax.set_xlim(START, END)
ax.set_xticks(pd.date_range(START, "2026-07-01", freq="6MS"))       # a tick every 6 months
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%y"))         # "Jan-24"
```

- **Keeping rows.** `data[condition]` keeps the rows where the condition is
  true. Conditions are combined with `&` (and), each in brackets. The
  extracted workbooks often hold much more history than the chart shows: the
  daily data in [2.2](charts/fig-2-2.qmd) start in 2010.
- **Tick dates.** `pd.date_range(start, end, freq=...)` makes the tick dates.
  `"MS"` means *month start*, so `"6MS"` is every six months and `"2MS"`
  every two.
- **Labels.** `DateFormatter("%b-%y")` writes each date as abbreviated month
  and two-digit year, as Excel does with the format `mmm-yy`.
- **Text dates.** If dates are stored as text, `pd.to_datetime(...)` converts
  them.
- **Shifting a date.** Use `pd.Timedelta(days=12)`, for example to place a
  label just left of a vertical line.

Used in: [1.2.1](charts/fig-1-2-1.qmd), [1.2.2](charts/fig-1-2-2.qmd),
[2.2](charts/fig-2-2.qmd), [3.2](charts/fig-3-2.qmd),
[3.4](charts/fig-3-4.qmd), [6.1](charts/fig-6-1.qmd).

## Tick marks and axis lines {#sec-ticks}

```python
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.3, pad=6)
```

`tick_params` sets the look of the tick marks and their labels:

- `direction="in"` makes the ticks point into the plot, as Excel's default
  does.
- `length` is the length of the ticks, in points. `length=0` hides them but
  keeps the labels.
- `pad` is the gap between the tick and its label.
- `labelsize` is the font size of the labels.
- `labelrotation` turns the labels.

The axis lines themselves are *spines*. `ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)`
hides the bottom one, which is usually done when an axis line is drawn
elsewhere, at zero (next section).

## An axis line at zero, with tick marks {#sec-axis-line}

When a chart has negative values, Excel draws the horizontal axis *at zero*,
with its tick marks there, while the labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
matplotlib has no such option, so the scripts build it from three pieces:

```python
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.9)              # the axis line at zero
ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.035, color="black", linewidth=0.7)     # short ticks pointing up
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)                   # no line at the bottom
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=7)                # labels at the bottom, no ticks
```

`ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.035)` draws a vertical line from 0 to 0.035 *in data
units* at each position in `x`. The tick length is therefore set in the
units of the y-axis. On a scale from -1 to 0.6 a tick of 0.035 is short, but
on a scale from -15 to 15 you need around 0.5. Ticks pointing down go from a
small negative number to 0: `ax.vlines(x, -0.12, 0)`.

The same trick works at any level: [3.1](charts/fig-3-1.qmd) draws its axis
line at 100. [6.2](charts/fig-6-2.qmd) does the same for the y-axis, a
vertical line at zero with horizontal ticks.

Used in: [1.1.2](charts/fig-1-1-2.qmd), [1.2.3](charts/fig-1-2-3.qmd),
[2.1](charts/fig-2-1.qmd), [3.1](charts/fig-3-1.qmd),
[3.3](charts/fig-3-3.qmd), [5.2](charts/fig-5-2.qmd),
[8](charts/fig-8-0.qmd), [10.2](charts/fig-10-2.qmd),
[11.1](charts/fig-11-1.qmd), [11.2](charts/fig-11-2.qmd).

## A right-hand scale {#sec-right-scale}

A series whose name ends in "(right scale)" is drawn on a second y-axis. The
second axis is a twin of the first: it shares the x-axis, and has its own
y-axis on the right.

```python
ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (100, 220), 30)     # from chart_style
ax_right.plot(dates, data["Gold (right scale)"], color="#FFA500")
```

There are two things to watch for.

**The legend.** Each axes object keeps its own list of labelled series, so
`ax.legend()` would only list the left-scale series. The scripts therefore
build the legend entries by hand. They make one short sample line
(`Line2D`) per series and pass them with their names:

```python
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

styles = {**left_series, usa: usa_colour}          # all series, in legend order
ax_right.legend([Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8) for c in styles.values()],
                list(styles))
```

`{**a, key: value}` builds a new dictionary from all entries of `a` plus one
more. The legend is put on `ax_right` because that axes object is drawn on
top, so nothing covers the legend.

**Drawing order.** The twin axes object lies on top of the original, so
right-scale series cover left-scale ones. If the left-scale series should be
on top, as in [3.2](charts/fig-3-2.qmd), swap the layers. The left axes
object also has to be made transparent, or it would hide the right one:

```python
ax.set_zorder(ax_right.get_zorder() + 1)
ax.patch.set_visible(False)        # the left plot area's white background
```

Used in: [1.1.1](charts/fig-1-1-1.qmd), [1.2.1](charts/fig-1-2-1.qmd),
[1.3.1](charts/fig-1-3-1.qmd), [3.2](charts/fig-3-2.qmd),
[3.4](charts/fig-3-4.qmd), [5.1](charts/fig-5-1.qmd),
[7.1](charts/fig-7-1.qmd), [10.1](charts/fig-10-1.qmd),
[13](charts/fig-13-0.qmd), [14.1](charts/fig-14-1.qmd).

## Stacked bars {#sec-stacked}

`ax.bar()` draws each bar from 0 unless you pass `bottom=`. For stacked bars,
each series starts where the previous ones end. A running total takes care
of that:

```python
bottom = np.zeros(len(data))                 # start at zero
for series, colour in stack_colours.items():  # from the bottom of the stack up
    ax.bar(x, data[series], bottom=bottom, color=colour, label=series)
    bottom += data[series].to_numpy()         # the next series starts on top
```

The order of the dictionary is the stacking order, from the bottom up. To
match the published chart, compare its colours from bottom to top.

`.to_numpy()` turns the pandas column into a plain numpy array before it is
added. pandas would otherwise try to line the values up by row label.

This works for stacks of positive values. With negative values the two
programs differ:

- **matplotlib** draws a negative value downwards from the top of the stack
  so far.
- **Excel** stacks negative values separately, downwards from zero.

[9.1](charts/fig-9-1.qmd) shows how this is handled.

Used in: [1.2.1](charts/fig-1-2-1.qmd), [2.3](charts/fig-2-3.qmd),
[7.2](charts/fig-7-2.qmd), [9.1](charts/fig-9-1.qmd),
[16.2](charts/fig-16-2.qmd).

## Grouped bars {#sec-grouped}

For bars side by side, each series is shifted a little to the left or right
of the category position:

```python
bar_width = 0.82 / len(years)                          # the group takes 0.82 of a step
for i, year in enumerate(years):
    offset = (i - (len(years) - 1) / 2) * bar_width    # for three series: -1, 0, +1 bar widths
    ax.bar(x + offset, data[year], width=bar_width, color=year_colours[year], label=year)
```

`enumerate()` gives each item together with its number (0, 1, 2, ...). The
offset centres the group on the category position, whatever the number of
series.

Used in: [1.1.1](charts/fig-1-1-1.qmd), [3.3](charts/fig-3-3.qmd).

## Shaded bands from Excel's helper series {#sec-bands}

Excel cannot shade the area between two lines directly. Chart makers work
around this with a *stacked area* chart:

1. An invisible area goes from zero up to the lower edge of the band.
2. A coloured area is stacked on top of it, with a height equal to the width
   of the band.

The extracted data contain these helper series exactly as they are in the
Excel file. Their names are things like `Min` and `Min-Max Band`, `ci_lo`
and `range`, or `Dummy1` to `Dummy4`. The band edges are found by adding
them up, and `fill_between` shades the area between the edges:

```python
band_lower = data["Min"]
band_upper = data["Min"] + data["Min-Max Band"]
ax.fill_between(dates, band_lower, band_upper, color="#FCE5D6", linewidth=0)
```

With two bands, as in [1.1.2](charts/fig-1-1-2.qmd) and
[8](charts/fig-8-0.qmd), there are four helper series:

- the invisible base (`Dummy1`);
- the first band (`Dummy2`);
- an invisible gap (`Dummy3`);
- the second band (`Dummy4`).

The edges are running totals of these.

`linewidth=0` removes the outline that `fill_between` draws by default.
`alpha=` (between 0 and 1) makes a band partly transparent, so overlapping
bands show through.

Used in: [1.1.2](charts/fig-1-1-2.qmd), [1.2.2](charts/fig-1-2-2.qmd),
[1.2.3](charts/fig-1-2-3.qmd), [8](charts/fig-8-0.qmd),
[14.1](charts/fig-14-1.qmd), [15.2](charts/fig-15-2.qmd).

## Legends {#sec-legends}

**The simple case.** Give each series a `label=` when you draw it, then call
`ax.legend()`.

**Position.** `loc` names the corner of the legend that is anchored.
`bbox_to_anchor` gives the anchor point as fractions of the plot area, where
(0, 0) is bottom left and (1, 1) top right:

```python
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.05, 0.98))   # top-left corner near the top left
```

**Layout.** These arguments, all in units of the font size, control the
spacing:

| Argument | Sets |
|---|---|
| `ncol` | The number of columns |
| `handlelength`, `handleheight` | The size of the sample line or box |
| `handletextpad` | The gap between the sample and the text |
| `labelspacing` | The gap between rows |
| `columnspacing` | The gap between columns |

**Hand-made entries.** When the legend should show something other than
what was drawn, make the sample symbols yourself and pass them with the
names. Examples are a right-hand scale, a box for a bar series, or a symbol
with no fill:

```python
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

handles = [Patch(color="#0065A8"),                                   # a filled box
           Line2D([], [], color="black", linewidth=1.8),             # a line
           Line2D([], [], linestyle="none", marker="o", color="black")]  # a dot
ax.legend(handles, ["Labor", "Financing premium", "Real GDP growth"])
```

**Order in several columns.** matplotlib fills a multi-column legend *column
by column*, while Excel fills it *row by row*. To get Excel's order, reorder
the entries before passing them in. [2.3](charts/fig-2-3.qmd) and
[6.1](charts/fig-6-1.qmd) show how.

## Text, arrows and coordinates {#sec-text}

`ax.text(x, y, "label")` places text at a point given *in data units*: on a
date axis, x is a date. The alignment arguments `ha` (`"left"`, `"center"`,
`"right"`) and `va` (`"top"`, `"center"`, `"bottom"`) say which point of the
text sits at (x, y). Text can be styled with `fontsize`, `fontstyle="italic"`,
`fontweight="bold"` and `color`. A line break is `\n`.

Sometimes data units are not what you want. Then pass a different
`transform`, the coordinate system of the position:

| `transform=` | x is | y is | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | data | data | A label next to a point or line |
| `ax.transAxes` | 0–1 across the plot | 0–1 up the plot | A panel title just above the plot |
| `ax.get_xaxis_transform()` | data | 0–1 up the plot | Labels **below** the x-axis, under a category |
| `ax.get_yaxis_transform()` | 0–1 across the plot | data | Marks on the y-axis line |

With `get_xaxis_transform()`, y = 0 is the bottom of the plot and negative
values are below it. That is how labels and separators are placed under the
axis. Such elements need `clip_on=False`, because by default matplotlib
cuts off anything outside the plot area.

`ax.annotate()` draws text with a connecting line:

```python
ax.annotate("Jan-Sep", xy=(x0, y0), xytext=(x1, y1),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="#A6A6A6"))
```

`xy` is the point the line points at and `xytext` is where the text goes.
`arrowstyle="-"` gives a plain line and `"-|>"` a filled arrowhead. With
empty text (`""`), `annotate` simply draws an arrow, as in
[11.1](charts/fig-11-1.qmd).

## Tables of labels below the plot {#sec-label-tables}

Several REO charts have two or three rows of category labels under the bars,
separated by vertical lines. For example, a row of country groups with
"Growth" and "Inflation" below. Excel produces these with multi-level
categories. The scripts draw them with the coordinates from the previous
section:

```python
trans = ax.get_xaxis_transform()
for xi in np.arange(0.5, 11, 1):                                # between all bars
    depth = -0.16 if xi in (0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5, 8.5, 10.5) else -0.07
    ax.plot([xi, xi], [0, depth], color="black", linewidth=0.6,
            transform=trans, clip_on=False)                     # separator lines
for centre, year in zip(np.arange(1.5, 10, 2), years):
    ax.text(centre, -0.12, year, ha="center", va="center", transform=trans)
```

- **Separators.** The lines between groups are longer than the lines between
  bars, so they reach down to the second row.
- **Room.** The labels need space under the plot. That space is made with a
  larger `bottom_gap` in `new_chart()`.
- **Typed labels.** In several of these charts the labels are not in the
  extracted data and are typed into the script.
- **`zip()`.** It walks through two lists side by side: the first centre
  with the first year, and so on.

Used in: [7.2](charts/fig-7-2.qmd), [9.1](charts/fig-9-1.qmd),
[10.1](charts/fig-10-1.qmd), [12.1](charts/fig-12-1.qmd),
[13](charts/fig-13-0.qmd), [14.2](charts/fig-14-2.qmd).

## Several panels {#sec-panels}

Charts with two panels side by side ask `new_chart()` for two plot areas.
They describe each panel by its settings in a list, and draw both in one
loop:

```python
panels = [
    ("datal", "Ten-year Bond Yields", ...),    # left panel
    ("datar", "Sovereign Spreads", ...),       # right panel
]
fig, axes = new_chart(..., ncols=2, wspace=0.45)

for ax, (sheet, title, ...) in zip(axes, panels):
    data = read_chart_data(STEM, sheet)
    ...                                         # the same drawing code for both panels
```

Each panel has its own sheet in the workbook (`datal`, `datar`). Writing the
drawing code once guarantees the two panels look alike. Whatever differs
(sheet, titles, scales, colours) is in the `panels` list.

Used in: [1.3.1](charts/fig-1-3-1.qmd), [2.2](charts/fig-2-2.qmd),
[7.2](charts/fig-7-2.qmd), [14.2](charts/fig-14-2.qmd).

## Line styles {#sec-line-styles}

- **Dashes.** `linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5))` is a dotted line and `(0, (5, 2))` a
  dashed one. The pairs are the lengths of dash and gap, in multiples of the
  line width. The leading 0 is the offset at which the pattern starts.
- **Line ends.** `solid_capstyle="round"` rounds the ends of a line, which
  looks closer to Excel's thick lines. `"butt"` ends the line exactly at the
  last point.
- **Corners.** `solid_joinstyle="round"` rounds the corners where a line
  changes direction.
- **Gaps.** A missing value (`NaN`) in the data leaves a gap in the line, as
  in Excel.

## Number formats and tick spacing {#sec-number-formats}

```python
from matplotlib.ticker import FormatStrFormatter, MultipleLocator

ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(0.2))              # a tick every 0.2
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))       # one decimal: 0.0, 0.2, ...
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:.1f}")                        # the same, newer style
```

- **Tick spacing.** `MultipleLocator(step)` puts a tick at every multiple of
  `step` within the axis limits. `set_y_scale()` from `chart_style` does the
  same with explicit tick positions.
- **Decimals.** By default matplotlib shows as many decimals as needed. Many
  REO axes show a fixed number, such as 0.0, 0.2 and 0.4, and the formatter
  sets that. `".1f"` means one decimal place.
